title: The Back to School AI Stack, Rated
author: RatedEd
summary: This RatedEd review audits the free tiers of the five major classroom AI tools, Diffit, MagicSchool, Brisk Teaching, Curipod, and SchoolAI, on the premise that ed-tech free tiers are volatile and shift as companies pivot between courting individual teachers and courting district contracts. The author signed up for every tool from scratch and read each plan page directly rather than relying on marketing copy, finding that Diffit's leveled-reading workflow remains genuinely uncapped on free (though exporting requires payment), while MagicSchool's 80-plus tools stay unrestricted by feature but don't retain output history, meaning strong generated content can vanish before a teacher needs it again. The most significant finding is SchoolAI's quiet mid-July change, which dropped free accounts from routine classroom use to five total supervised-chat sessions per year, effectively converting it from a daily tool into a one-time evaluation window that will surprise anyone who built a routine around the old terms. The piece closes with a practical setup sequence, ordered from lowest-friction, most durable tools to the ones requiring the most caution, so a teacher spends limited setup time on the tools least likely to disappear mid-year.
points: The review's central finding is that free tiers across the five major classroom AI tools shifted meaningfully over the summer, generally tightening as companies moved from courting individual teachers to courting district contracts.
Diffit rates highest because its core leveled-reading workflow has no generation cap, though exporting to Google Docs requires a paid tier.
MagicSchool's free plan is uncapped by feature but doesn't save output history, meaning a strong lesson generated in September can't be retrieved again without being manually saved elsewhere.
SchoolAI is flagged as most disrupted: its free plan quietly dropped in July to five total 'Space' sessions per year, turning it from a daily classroom tool into an evaluation window.
The piece's practical contribution is a five-tool setup sequence ordered by lowest friction and least likely to be pulled out from under a teacher mid-year.
quotes: Free tiers in ed tech are the least stable thing in your entire toolkit. They get generous when a company is chasing teachers, and they get tight when the company starts chasing districts. Both of those things happened this summer.

Paste an article, a URL, a PDF, or just a topic, and Diffit hands back the same content at multiple reading levels with comprehension questions and vocabulary pulled from the passage itself. Second grade through high school, plus translation into a long list of languages.

The free tier caps how much you can generate, and it does not save your output history. That second one bites harder than it sounds: generate something great in September, want it again in January, and it is gone.

In mid-July, the free plan changed. Individual free accounts now get five Space launches per year. Not per month. Per year. Your onboarding Space does not count against it, and referrals earn two more sessions each, but the practical ceiling is roughly one Space per grading period.
Diffit charges you in exports. The work is unlimited, but getting it into Google Docs is not. MagicSchool charges you in memory. Generate freely, but do not expect to find it again.
Anyone who built a routine on the old always-free tier is going to hit a wall this fall and be surprised by it.
